passage: Shreya answered every call from home with "All good, Mummy, just busy." In her Pune flat she had stopped opening the curtains. Her flatmates seemed to juggle classes, internships and cooking dinner without a crack, and she felt like the only one sinking, a burden they were too polite to mention. So she smiled in the lift, laughed at the right moments and cried into a pillow at night. On Tuesday, after another sleepless night, she looked at the helpline number pinned on the fridge and then at Nazia Masi's name in her phone. Sitting alone with it and hoping it would fade had not worked for weeks. Her thumb shook. "Masi, can you talk today? I'm not okay," she typed, and sent it before she could delete it. The reply came within a minute: "Calling you now."

qa.q: Which city is Shreya's flat in?
Why does Shreya hide how bad things are?
qa.a: She feels ashamed, like a burden, and thinks her flatmates cope better than she does.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that was wise, and what could come next?
qa.a: She told a trusted adult the same day; next she could accept Nazia Masi's help in reaching a counsellor, a doctor or the helpline.

qa.q: How might Nazia Masi feel on getting that message?
qa.a: Probably worried, but glad to be trusted, which fits her calling straight away.

grounding: The protagonist feels like a burden and hides it, then reaches out to one trusted adult the same day instead of waiting alone.

passage:
In the Bengaluru PG, Anand smiled at breakfast and then lay on his bed all afternoon with the curtains shut. For weeks the thoughts had got heavier: everyone else manages, I'm just weak, they'd be better off without me dragging them down. When his mother called he said, "All fine, Amma, busy with project."

On Tuesday Jomon, his roommate, found him still in bed at four. "Anand. You've not eaten. Talk to me."

Anand almost said he was just tired. Then something cracked. "I'm just a weight on everyone. It's too much. I can't hold it by myself anymore."

Jomon sat on the bed. He didn't argue. He said, "Then let's not hold it alone. Now, together." He looked up the helpline, and Anand spoke to a counsellor for half an hour with Jomon beside him. That evening Anand called his mother and told her the truth.

qa.q: What did Anand tell his mother on the phone at first?
qa.a: He said, "All fine, Amma, busy with project."

qa.q: What was Anand feeling underneath his smiles at breakfast?
qa.a: Anand felt ashamed and worthless, believing he was a burden and weaker than everyone else.

qa.q: Why was calling the helpline that same day important?
qa.a: The feelings had become too heavy to carry alone, so reaching a counsellor that afternoon, with Jomon present, got Anand real support without waiting.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt finding Anand still in bed at four?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt worried and alarmed, which is why he sat with Anand and helped him call straight away.

grounding: The story shows a young man hiding how bad he feels out of shame who tells one person and calls a helpline the same day.

passage:
"You've said 'fine' four times tonight," Vandana said, handing Pallavi a cup of tea in the hostel pantry.

"Because I am fine."

"You haven't come to class in a week."

Pallavi looked at the tea. "Everyone else is managing, didi. You're managing. I'm just... I'm the weak one. I don't want to bother anyone."

"You're not bothering me. Tell me how bad it is. Honestly."

A long pause. "Bad. Really bad. Some nights I wish I could just disappear."

Vandana set her own cup down. "Thank you for telling me. That's too heavy to carry alone. Will you come with me to the counselling centre now? It's open till eight."

"Now?"

"Now. I'll sit outside the door."

Pallavi wiped her face with her sleeve. "Okay."

They walked across the dark campus together, and the counsellor saw her at seven-thirty.

qa.q: Until what time was the counselling centre open?
What was Pallavi feeling when she said she was the weak one?
qa.a: Pallavi felt ashamed and like a burden, comparing herself to others and not wanting to bother anyone.

qa.q: Why was Vandana right to go to the counselling centre that same evening?
qa.a: Pallavi said she sometimes wished to disappear, so getting her to a counsellor that night, with company, was safer than waiting.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when Pallavi said it was really bad?
qa.a: Vandana was likely frightened but steady, choosing to thank Pallavi and act right away instead of panicking.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young woman who feels like a burden and hides her pain, telling one trusted person and getting help the same evening.
